A lot of people think I'm a huge asshole because of how often I use obscure huge words.

Basically every time I hear a new word I have to figure out what it means and see if I want to work it into my lexicon. I hate not knowing what word to use in specific situations, and will frequently take a long pause in the middle of a sentence to assess what words would work in the sentence, and the implications of using those words as opposed to other, simpler words.

I find that in my attempts to ensure that people don't misunderstand me, I cause total lack of understanding. Where before they could have figured out my intentions based on context, all meaning is lost when they hear a word they just don't know.

The worst part about this, is some of the people I talk to (immediate family) get offended because they think I'm being uppity.

How do you react to hearing a word you don't understand?
Are people of a sesquipedalian nature aggravating to you?
'What the fuck does [x] mean?' 'It means ---' 'oh, that's cool, I'll steal that word for future use'

I used to do the same thing, using words is a great way to make sure they stay in your vocabulary. I encountered the same problem you have. You come off as arrogant whether you like it or not. People always think you're talking down to them just due to your choice in words. The worst is when you use a word you consider relatively simple and somebody gives you shit. I was given some advice by somebody I have a lot of respect for to tone it down especially when talking to women. Try to keep it simple in everyday conversations is my advice to you. It sucks to dumb down your speech, but it beats coming off as somebody who thinks their better than everybody else.

Language is about communication and the best way of expressing ideas to another. That means it does need to be tailored to one's audience. I love coming across new words and expanding my vocabulary and with English I'm particularly interested in etymology too, given the mongrel way in which the language developed. However a conversation is rarely the place to do this, because it fragments the discussion if someone has to ask and (generally) they'll avoid doing so either to keep the conversation moving or to avoid embarrassment.

As a result, using obscure words in speech is actually poor use of language because you end up failing to communicate effectively.

Written language is ideal for expanding vocabulary because you take it at your own pace and can check words as needed. It's the reason reading is still so essential, and even audiobooks don't cut it. I was particularly impressed by Kindle's (and most likely other e-readers before it) integrated feature of immediately popping up dictionary definitions and etymology when you click on a word.

Still be aware of your target audience with written English but feel more free to use more elaborate language than when speaking.
